linkedin.label: Counter-Intuitive Thesis
linkedin.text:
When an AI agent pulls the wrong spreadsheet, the model is rarely to blame.

The brain simply never saw your team's conventions. Like a senior data scientist transferring from Google Maps to Google Sheets, the model knows statistics and forecasting but lacks your team's onboarding doc.

In agent architecture, that onboarding doc splits into two distinct layers: an always-on playbook (CLAUDE.md or GEMINI.md) loaded on every request, and on-demand SKILL.md folders loaded through progressive disclosure only when triggered.

linkedin.label: Concrete Analogy
linkedin.text:
Imagine a data scientist transferring from Google Maps to Google Sheets on day one.

He has the same badge and laptop, and knows how to define metrics. Yet he still does not know which dashboards matter at Sheets or what the fifty team OKRs are.

Your AI agent is in that exact position until you write its playbook. Here is how harnesses inject CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md, and progressive-disclosure SKILL.md files into the model's context.

linkedin.label: Practitioner Question
linkedin.text:
Where should your team's fifty analytical procedures live inside an AI agent?

Pasting all fifty into CLAUDE.md or GEMINI.md burns tokens on every turn. Because the harness loads that file on every request, keep it to a one-page summary of universal rules—like running data quality checks before regression.

Move the full six-gate procedures, SQL templates, and Python scripts into SKILL.md folders so the harness loads them only when the task matches.

linkedin.label: Verbatim Quote + Synthesis
linkedin.text:
"Check the onboarding before you blame the brain."

At startup, a harness only loads each skill's name and one-sentence description. Full procedures and reference SQL stay on disk until the model explicitly requests them.

If that one-sentence description in SKILL.md is vague, the brain never opens the skill—making playbook writing the highest-leverage work a domain expert can do.

x.label: Hard Truth Opener
x.text:
When an AI agent defines "active customer" wrong, you have an onboarding failure.

The model weights are frozen. Until you put team rules in CLAUDE.md or GEMINI.md, the agent is a new hire without an onboarding doc.

x.label: Mechanism Shift
x.text:
How agent playbooks manage token budgets:

→ Always-on (CLAUDE.md / GEMINI.md): Loaded on every turn for universal team rules.
→ On-demand (SKILL.md): Only the 1-sentence description loads at startup; full SQL & gates load only when matched.

x.text:
When evaluating an AI agent, test how much you can teach it:

Can you write an always-on file? Can you add modular SKILL.md folders with progressive disclosure? And can you take both to a different harness without lock-in?

linkedin.text:
Developers never gave LLMs the ability to open files or browse the web.

They taught the model a new kind of sentence. An LLM API only accepts a model name and a list of messages, returning pure text from frozen weights.

When you ask for NVDA's closing price, the model outputs a formatted string like get_stock_price(ticker="NVDA"). External software runs that function and hands the result back—turning a sealed prediction engine into an agent with hands.

linkedin.label: Concrete Analogy
linkedin.text:
Think of an LLM on its own as a brain locked inside a skull.

Your brain can decide to pick up a cup, but without your hand, nothing moves. An LLM faces the same constraint: its knowledge is frozen the day training ends, and its API only sends and receives text.

To build an agent, developers surround that rented brain with body parts—tools like read_file, write_file, and run_shell_command that act as its hands and eyes.

linkedin.label: Practitioner Question
linkedin.text:
What happens inside the codebase when a team switches from Claude to Gemini?

Through OpenRouter, switching models takes changing one line of text. Because the LLM is rented by the token through a fixed API contract, "model": "anthropic/claude-..." simply becomes "model": "google/gemini-...".

The rest of the application code and tool definitions—Read, Edit, Bash, or web_fetch—stay untouched while the new brain brings its own speed and cost profile.

When you calculate 72 × 98 on a calculator, it has no idea why you are asking. Agent tools work the exact same way.

In Gemini CLI or Claude Code, tools like read_file, Edit, and Bash are plain code functions described in English on a menu. The LLM writes the text request; the tool executes blindly.

Claude in your browser and Claude Code in your terminal share the same brain.

Slack's API speaks in channels and threads, while GitHub's speaks in pull requests.

That made me wonder how much of that capital funds real technical differentiation versus a hot buzzword and a compelling story. Before writing a check, every investor should ask: What happens the day OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google ships your product for free?

runs.t: Before asking this question, investors should understand the difference between a wrapper and a moat. Both words get thrown around in AI pitches and are rarely used correctly. Strictly speaking, “wrapper” describes a layer of a product, not the whole company. It refers specifically to the AI capability, which belongs entirely to the LLM provider, such as Anthropic. The startup formats its users’ requests and sends them to a rented model via an Application Programming Interface, or API, then formats the response it gets back. Think of an API as a waiter taking an order: the startup packages the customer’s request, hands it to the kitchen (the LLM vendor), and carries the dish back to the table. They don’t own the kitchen.

runs.t: Given that nearly every AI startup is a wrapper at the AI layer, the real work for an investor is figuring out whether there’s a moat somewhere else. First, look for a product that gets smarter with every use. If you call GPT-5 a million times, it doesn’t make your product smarter than a competitor’s, since OpenAI improves that model for every customer at once. For the product to actually get smarter, the improvements have to be stored somewhere the company owns. There are three ways a startup can do that: fine-tuning on proprietary data, retrieval-based knowledge accumulation, and feedback loops.

blocks.text: Fine-Tuning on Proprietary Data

runs.t: Fine-tuning on proprietary data means periodically retraining a model on accumulated, company-owned interaction data so that it gets better at the specific task it’s meant to do. The process begins with an already-trained base model, like Gemini. The startup feeds a proprietary, expert-labeled dataset to the model, adjusting its parameters to master the specific task.

runs.t: Say a startup builds an AI tool for reviewing insurance claims. Every claim it processes, along with the human adjuster’s final decision, becomes a new training example. Over thousands of claims, the model gets better at spotting the specific patterns that matter to that insurer, in a way a generic model never would. If the dataset is something only the startup has access to, such as years of real customer interactions, regulated-industry transaction data, or outcomes from real cases handled, then this is a moat. Even if a competitor copies the fine-tuning process, they can’t get the same data.

runs.t: A second way startups build this kind of moat is retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG. Unlike fine-tuning, retrieval leaves the model untouched and instead focuses on growing the database the model uses to answer questions. In practice, the system continuously logs user interactions and outcomes. Each time a new user has a question, the system searches the database for the most relevant matches and hands them to the AI as context before it responds.

runs.t: Let’s take the example of a startup that sells AI customer support for e-commerce companies. On day one, the AI answers a ticket using only general knowledge, since it doesn’t yet know anything specific about that company. It then stores the entire resolution context, including what happened, whether a refund was issued, and the applicable policy. By ticket fifty thousand, a similar situation comes in, and now the AI retrieves actual past resolutions from that exact company, including edge cases nobody wrote into an official policy document. The answer gets better, not because the AI got smarter, but because the archive it’s pulling from got deeper. This is the moat, since the archive is built entirely from proprietary interactions competitors don’t have.

blocks.text: Signal 2: How Hard Is It to Leave?

runs.t: Start by checking integration depth: how difficult it would be for an existing customer to stop using the startup’s product and switch to another one. If a product offers no proprietary data and no deep integration, the customer can easily switch to another wrapper. However, if the product is deeply integrated into a customer’s existing systems, such as their CRM, single sign-on, or approval workflows, and has historical data or team habits built around it, switching becomes much harder. The AI itself might still be entirely rented. The switching cost comes from somewhere else: the customer’s data, workflows, and habits, not the intelligence layer at all.

Imagine standing at the top of a mountain blindfolded, feeling for the steepest path down.

Step by step, it descends into a mathematical valley where prediction errors are smallest.
